The post Stunning New Opera House Opens With a Gravity-Defying Grand Staircase (LOOK) appeared first on Good News Network.

Actual Article Body:
Despite its curtain raising rather late in the year, Shanghai’s new opera house has elbowed its way to the front row of international architectural debuts—thanks to a gravity-defying grand staircase.

Rising above the banks of the Huangpu River, commission for the Grand Opera House was awarded 10 years ago to Norwegian architecture firm Snøhetta.

The team from Snøhetta reasoned that despite being architectural and design marvels in many cases, opera houses naturally contain many “thresholds” that limit the ability of people to appreciate and interact with a building. Their hope was to remove these thresholds when possible and create greater harmony with the civic environment in which the hall is set.

Nothing could epitomize this more than the head-turning spiral staircase on the building’s exterior, drawing visitors towards the heart of its crescent floorplan. It positions itself right along the network of riverside thoroughfares, and allows anyone, ticket holders or otherwise, to climb its Chinese fan-inspired heights up to an observation platform with clear line of sight to the marvelous central business district.

Symphonies are divided into movements, and movement acts as both an architectural and social connector at the opera house, a statement from the firm details, and shapes the ways people approach, enter, and move through the building.

The 1.6 million-square-foot (146,786-square-meter) opera house will accommodate a broad spectrum of performances, from traditional opera and classical music to experimental productions conceived for new and diverse audiences.

With 3 auditoriums and a total seating capacity of 4,200, it brings performance, rehearsal, production, education, exhibition, and hospitality together under one roof.

The Harmony auditorium is awash in red and contains 5 levels and 3 terraces with seating for 2,000 people. The hall functions as a finely tuned instrument, combining state-of-the-art theatre systems with carefully calibrated acoustics thanks to design partner Nagata Acoustics.

The second auditorium, called the Soar Theater, accommodates 1,200 seats and offers a more intimate setting for smaller-scale production. It is particularly suited to baroque and classical opera, operetta, regional production, and theatre. It’s likely to host many of the traditional Chinese operas called Xiqu.

The 1,000-seat third auditorium, called the Open Stage, supports experimental and flexible performance formats through adaptable stage and seating configurations. It can host traditional and non-traditional production with a stage backlit by floor to ceiling windows that look out upon the river and city beyond whilst flooding the hall with natural light.

The opening was last weekend, with a performance of the immortal Italian classic Tosca, ironically the most famous opera of Giacomo Puccini that isn’t set in China.

This weekend features Verdi’s Aida, and it’s just 3 weeks before Americans will make their debut there, with the American Ballet Company bringing out Swan Lake just in time to get excited for winter.

I am terrified of heights and could never climb that staircase, but I can appreciate how good it looks.

White House defends Trump after archbishop calls prayer moment 'manipulated' ahead of midterms

Archbishop Jeffrey Grob accused the White House of manipulating video of an Oval Office prayer with Catholic bishops for political gain before midterms.

Actual Article Body:

President Donald Trump joins Catholic bishops and archbishops for a moment of prayer inside the Oval Office.

The White House on Monday defended President Donald Trump after Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob publicly apologized for participating in an Oval Office prayer with the president, accusing the administration of using the religious gathering for political purposes less than two weeks before the midterm elections.

Grob issued a statement Sunday titled "A Public Apology," alleging that the White House distributed photographs and video of the Thursday prayer without the consent of the 12 participating bishops. He accused the administration of manipulating a sacred moment. The archbishop said he had received messages from Catholics concerned that the prayer appeared to constitute a political endorsement. Grob acknowledged having reservations before attending and apologized for the distress his participation caused.

"I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way," he said. "We came in good faith to try to work for the betterment of our fellow human beings, to ease their suffering, to build up the common good, and to pray with a president, not to pose for a political photo opportunity to benefit the few."

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers defended Trump's record on religious liberty and Catholic priorities in a statement to Fox News Digital following the archbishop's public apology.

BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: MY YEAR WITH DOJ'S RELIGIOUS LIBERTY COMMISSION: WHY I SAID YES

Jeffrey S. Grob, Archbishop of Milwaukee, penned an open letter apologizing for any harms caused by his meeting with President Trump last week. At the meeting with Trump, he says photos were taken of a prayer with fellow bishops and shared on social media without their consent. (Margo Martin/X)

"There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it: he stopped the weaponization of the federal government against Christians, proudly defended and expanded our religious rights, pardoned pro-life activists, stopped the chemical mutilation of our nation’s children, and protected parents’ rights," she said.

The meeting, which Grob said was arranged by the Heritage Foundation, was intended to address immigration enforcement, religious worker visas and other Catholic priorities. Following a 90-minute discussion with White House domestic policy staff and advisors, the bishops entered the Oval Office, where Trump presented commemorative tokens before they prayed together. Grob said the group was unaware that video was being recorded.

Des Moines Bishop William Joensen also criticized the gathering's subsequent publicity in a statement published Saturday, saying the bishops never intended to endorse a political candidate or party.

"None of us bishops were unaware that our meeting was on the cusp of a national election. Yet in no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," he said. "That said, in retrospect, I would have done well to be more mindful of Jesus’ admonition: ‘Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves; so be shrewd as serpents and simple as doves’ (Matthew 10:16). I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes."

POPE LEO SLAMS THOSE WHO 'MANIPULATE RELIGION' FOR MILITARY OR POLITICAL GAIN, TRUMP RESPONDS

Denver Archbishop James Golka, who led the prayer, discussed his participation in an interview with the Denver Catholic. Golka acknowledged concerns about the video's political implications but emphasized that praying for elected officials remains a longstanding Catholic practice.

"I wasn’t sure what to do. On one hand, it was a great opportunity to raise important issues for the Church’s benefit," he said. "On the other hand, I knew people might be upset. Though I originally thought it would be a private meeting, I knew that it could be shared and that some might use it for political purposes.

"But as I prayed about it, I thought that this is what Catholics do," he continued. "We pray for people. No matter whether we agree or disagree on anything, we always pray for our country and leaders."

The controversy comes as Catholic leaders continue to disagree with the Trump administration over some of its policies, particularly immigration. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops sued the administration in February 2025 over the suspension of refugee resettlement funding.

Other prominent Catholic leaders have encouraged continued engagement with the administration. In a May interview with Fox News Digital, Bishop Robert Barron, a member of Trump's Religious Liberty Commission, cautioned against demonizing the president despite disagreements over immigration and other policies.

"What I don't want from the church is a kind of demonization of the Trump administration," he said.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

Bishop Robert Barron warned against the "demonization" of the Trump administration and encouraged dialogue between Catholic leaders and the White House amid disagreements over immigration policies. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Archdiocese of Milwaukee declined to comment further on the matter when reached by Fox News Digital.

Exclusive — White House: Trump’s Energy Infusing Republicans with Midterm Boost

Trump’s relentless campaign schedule in the home stretch before the midterm elections is something the White House says gives Republicans their best shot at emerging victorious.
The post Exclusive — White House: Trump’s Energy Infusing Republicans with Midterm Boost appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump’s relentless campaign schedule in the home stretch before the midterm elections is something the White House says gives Republicans their best shot at emerging victorious next week.

Trump is and has been hosting rallies in battleground states and districts from coast to coast—Alaska one day, Texas another, North Carolina or Florida on the next, and everywhere in between—aimed at firing up the GOP base and driving up Trump voter turnout. Listening to any Republican strategist or candidate ahead of the elections next Tuesday, therein lies the issue for the GOP ahead of November 3: Republicans have to turn out their voters to have a chance. Enthusiasm is high on the Democrat side, for sure, given the national environment, and in any normal midterm election the party out of power like the Democrats this cycle would be expected to take sweeping majorities in both chambers of Congress. But the races are tightening everywhere, especially in U.S. Senate battlegrounds, and late August through September polling surges for Democrats in many of them are falling and races are reverting to the mean—meaning Republicans have a decent shot at hanging on to many seats that looked like they may have been lost just a couple weeks ago.

President Donald J. Trump speaks to members of the media before boarding Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House, en route to Michigan for a midterm rally, Sunday, October 25, 2026. (Official White House Photo by Patrick Witty)

“It is incredible to see President Trump criss cross the country working tirelessly to help elect Republicans. And because of that, they are in a much better position to beat back the Dumocrats and their radical leftist agenda,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, told Breitbart News exclusively on Monday. “His energy and commitment to get Republicans elected is no surprise because he has been doing it from Day One. Nobody should doubt the power of his endorsement, and nobody should ever question the effectiveness of his rallies. The love and support he receives from sold out arenas and packed stadiums prove the MAGA movement is stronger than ever before.”

Cheung is exactly correct that there has never been another endorsement like Trump’s backing, and his rallies have been throughout his decade atop the GOP one of the singular greatest forces for unleashing grassroots support and energy for those he campaigns with. The big challenge facing Republicans in key U.S. Senate and U.S. House battlegrounds is whether it is enough to hang on in the face of headwinds that normally see the opposition sweep into some kind of power. Only twice in the last century has a party with a trifecta bolstered their majorities in the first midterm elections of a president’s term, in 1934 amid the Great Depression and Democrat President Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s unveiling of the New Deal and then again in 2002 in the aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks when George W. Bush’s Republicans were fighting the War on Terror. Perhaps Trump’s decade plus of leading Republicans, and all the weaponization by Democrats who promise to go for a third round of impeachment against him if they win, is enough to rise to that level of historical anomaly to defy history itself. But either way, Trump campaigning in all these places is easily the best thing Republicans could ask for. In especially redder states, the pathway to victory for the GOP is getting Republicans out to vote—not rocket science—and the best thing to ensure that happens is to get the president there and directly involved.

Trump has an action-packed closing schedule, as does Vice President JD Vance, ahead of next Tuesday:

And amazingly, with Republicans unleashing Trump as their key weapon ahead of next Tuesday, Democrats have instead had to turn to former President Barack Obama to energize their base. Obama, who has been out of office for a decade, may help Democrats in some urban centers but the degrading nature of his comments, like the one he made this weekend about Trump allegedly turning the White House into the Cheesecake Factory, have significant potential to further backfire and fire up Republicans almost as much as Trump’s energy campaigning in these places does.

Exclusive — White House: Trump’s Energy Infusing Republicans with Midterm Boost

Trump’s relentless campaign schedule in the home stretch before the midterm elections is something the White House says gives Republicans their best shot at emerging victorious.
The post Exclusive — White House: Trump’s Energy Infusing Republicans with Midterm Boost appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump’s relentless campaign schedule in the home stretch before the midterm elections is something the White House says gives Republicans their best shot at emerging victorious next week.

Trump is and has been hosting rallies in battleground states and districts from coast to coast—Alaska one day, Texas another, North Carolina or Florida on the next, and everywhere in between—aimed at firing up the GOP base and driving up Trump voter turnout. Listening to any Republican strategist or candidate ahead of the elections next Tuesday, therein lies the issue for the GOP ahead of November 3: Republicans have to turn out their voters to have a chance. Enthusiasm is high on the Democrat side, for sure, given the national environment, and in any normal midterm election the party out of power like the Democrats this cycle would be expected to take sweeping majorities in both chambers of Congress. But the races are tightening everywhere, especially in U.S. Senate battlegrounds, and late August through September polling surges for Democrats in many of them are falling and races are reverting to the mean—meaning Republicans have a decent shot at hanging on to many seats that looked like they may have been lost just a couple weeks ago.

President Donald J. Trump speaks to members of the media before boarding Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House, en route to Michigan for a midterm rally, Sunday, October 25, 2026. (Official White House Photo by Patrick Witty)

“It is incredible to see President Trump criss cross the country working tirelessly to help elect Republicans. And because of that, they are in a much better position to beat back the Dumocrats and their radical leftist agenda,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, told Breitbart News exclusively on Monday. “His energy and commitment to get Republicans elected is no surprise because he has been doing it from Day One. Nobody should doubt the power of his endorsement, and nobody should ever question the effectiveness of his rallies. The love and support he receives from sold out arenas and packed stadiums prove the MAGA movement is stronger than ever before.”

Cheung is exactly correct that there has never been another endorsement like Trump’s backing, and his rallies have been throughout his decade atop the GOP one of the singular greatest forces for unleashing grassroots support and energy for those he campaigns with. The big challenge facing Republicans in key U.S. Senate and U.S. House battlegrounds is whether it is enough to hang on in the face of headwinds that normally see the opposition sweep into some kind of power. Only twice in the last century has a party with a trifecta bolstered their majorities in the first midterm elections of a president’s term, in 1934 amid the Great Depression and Democrat President Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s unveiling of the New Deal and then again in 2002 in the aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks when George W. Bush’s Republicans were fighting the War on Terror. Perhaps Trump’s decade plus of leading Republicans, and all the weaponization by Democrats who promise to go for a third round of impeachment against him if they win, is enough to rise to that level of historical anomaly to defy history itself. But either way, Trump campaigning in all these places is easily the best thing Republicans could ask for. In especially redder states, the pathway to victory for the GOP is getting Republicans out to vote—not rocket science—and the best thing to ensure that happens is to get the president there and directly involved.

And amazingly, with Republicans unleashing Trump as their key weapon ahead of next Tuesday, Democrats have instead had to turn to former President Barack Obama to energize their base. Obama, who has been out of office for a decade, may help Democrats in some urban centers but the degrading nature of his comments, like the one he made this weekend about Trump allegedly turning the White House into the Cheesecake Factory, have significant potential to further backfire and fire up Republicans almost as much as Trump’s energy campaigning in these places does.
